one_liner: Go AVX2 assembly comparing one value against a column into a bitmask; 5-232x faster than its scalar Go loop.
what_it_does: A Go package that compares one search value against every element of a []uint8, []uint16, []uint32, []uint64, []float32 or []float64 slice and writes the results as a packed bitmap: bit i of dst is set when the predicate holds for rows[i]. It offers Equals, NotEquals, GreaterThan, LessThan, GreaterEquals and LesserEquals for all six types, plus IsNaN for floats. Functions come typed (VectorEquals8, VectorGreaterThanFloat64 and so on) and as generic wrappers that dispatch through a type switch. The scalar loop in the README is the exact semantic reference, so the package replaces that kind of hand-written filter loop directly.
how_it_is_fast: Each kernel loads 2 or 4 YMM registers per iteration (64 bytes for 8-bit and 16/32-bit lanes, 128 bytes for 64-bit lanes) and compares them against a broadcast of the search value. Integers use VPCMPEQ/VPCMPGT; unsigned ordering is done by XOR-flipping the sign bit of both sides. Floats use VCMPPS/VCMPPD with ordered or unordered quiet predicates that match Go's NaN semantics. VPMOVMSKB packs the compare results into a general register, BMI2 PEXT drops the duplicate bits for 16/32/64-bit lanes, and whole bytes are stored to dst. Missing predicates come from swapping operands and NOT-ing the mask. The assembly is produced by an avo generator (internal/avo/avo.go). An AVX1 128-bit variant uses VPSHUFB instead of PEXT, and the dispatcher picks a path at run time through golang.org/x/sys/cpu, or at compile time with GOAMD64=v3, then sends the tail to the scalar loop.
when_to_use: In-memory columnar filtering in Go: evaluating `column <op> constant` over unsigned or float slices of thousands of rows or more to build a selection bitmap.
amd64 hosts with AVX2 and BMI2 (Haswell and Zen or newer); build with GOAMD64=v3 to drop the run-time feature check.
Predicates whose match pattern defeats branch prediction. With about one third random matches the README shows 53x geomean and 232x for 8-bit Equals over the scalar loop on an i9-14900.
Scanning float columns for NaNs: VectorIsNaNFloat32 and VectorIsNaNFloat64 are 10.6x and 5.4x even against a well-predicted scalar loop (derived from page data).
When you want a tiny, vendorable dependency: BSD-2-Clause, the only run-time dependency is golang.org/x/sys, and the assembly is generated and checked in.
when_not_to_use: arm64 and other non-amd64 targets: they get only the scalar loop (CI just checks that arm64 builds), and there is no NEON or AVX-512 path.

Signed integer columns with ordered comparisons. Only unsigned and float element types exist, and reinterpreting int32 as uint32 makes negative values compare as large. Equals and NotEquals still work after a reinterpret cast.
Short slices. Below 64 (8-bit), 32 (16-bit) or 16 (32/64-bit) rows the AVX2 path is skipped, and any remainder runs through the scalar loop.
Range predicates, multi-column filters, or accumulating into an existing bitmap. Each call rewrites dst from bit 0 and zeroes its unused tail, so you have to AND or OR the separate bitmaps yourself.

Columns much larger than cache. The benchmark's 66-533 KB inputs are cache-resident, so gains on DRAM-resident data will be capped by memory bandwidth; this was not measured. Also avoid versions before cb1b7b5 (2025-10-03), whose ordered unsigned comparisons were wrong for values with the top bit set.

integration.dependencies: golang.org/x/sys (CPU feature detection); github.com/mmcloughlin/avo v0.6.0 only to regenerate the assembly
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.18 per go.mod (generics); CI builds and tests with Go 1.20; regenerating the assembly needs Go 1.22.5 per internal/avo/go.mod
integration.platforms: amd64 with AVX2+BMI2 (256-bit path) or AVX only (128-bit path); every other GOARCH and the purego build tag use the scalar loop
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The functions keep no state (CPU flags are read once at package init) and write only to the caller's dst slice, so concurrent calls with separate dst buffers are safe by construction.

gotchas: Operand order reads backwards from SQL: VectorGreaterThan sets bit i when search > rows[i], so it selects rows less than search, and VectorLessThan selects rows greater than search. The godoc says this, but the names invite the opposite reading.

dst must hold at least len(rows) bits, or the call panics with 'vectorcmp: given bitmap is not large enough to hold bits for all rows'. The bounds check was only added before the assembly call in 2ef0089 (2025-03-04); older versions could write past a short dst. NaN handling was fixed in 86570d6 (2024-10-30) and unsigned ordering in cb1b7b5 (2025-10-03), so pin a recent commit.

Tests compare the assembly against the scalar loop 500 times in each of four CI configurations (default, GOAMD64=v3, AVX1 tag, purego). Every input uses only the values 'a'/'b'/'c', the type maximum and NaN, with search always 'b' and lengths of 65,536-67,583, so short slices and other search values (0, max, NaN as the search) are never exercised. Reading the generated kernels found the predicate codes, operand order and bit packing consistent with the scalar loop; no bug was found.

Harness flaw: the baseline is the library's own branchy scalar Go loop, run on data with about one-third random matches, so it costs about 2.2 ns per element, against about 0.35 ns per element in the well-predicted IsNaN rows. Using the IsNaN scalar time (about 23.6 us) as a proxy for a predictable-branch loop, the SIMD gain is roughly 25-38x for 8-bit, 13-18x for 16-bit, 7-11x for 32-bit and 3.5-5.4x for 64-bit lanes (derived from page data, cross-row estimate), not 53-232x. The table also predates the 2025-10-04/05 optimisation commits f74d5a7 and 3ff822d.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it when you need a per-row predicate bitmap from a numeric column. go-byte-test only answers whether all bytes equal one value, so it is not a substitute. go-and (bitmap AND/OR/XOR) and go-popcount or pospop (counting set bits) are the natural next steps in the same filter pipeline, not alternatives.
verified_claims_summary: The README's benchstat table (n=10, i9-14900, GOMAXPROCS 32, Go version not stated) runs the same benchmarks built with the purego tag (scalar Go loop, gc compiler) and with the default AVX2 dispatch. Each run uses 65,536-67,583 random elements drawn from 'a'/'b'/'c' with search 'b'. 8-bit Equals drops from 145.6 us to 0.628 us (about 232x), 64-bit Equals from 146.6 us to 4.47 us (about 33x), and the geomean is 133.0 us to 2.49 us (about 53x). The IsNaN rows, where the scalar branch is predictable, give 10.6x (float32) and 5.4x (float64) (derived from page data).
status_note: Stale (last commit 2025-10-05, 29 commits, 4 stars), but small, BSD-2-Clause, dependent only on x/sys and CI-tested in four build configurations, so it is easy to vendor. The headline numbers are inflated by a branch-mispredicting scalar baseline, which is the main harness flaw, and the README's Go Reference badge points at the Jille/vectorcmp fork rather than the github.com/hexon/vectorcmp module path.
